crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: FAIR Data
children.blurb: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for making research data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable, published in 2016 as the FAIR Guiding Principles.

children.name: Metadata and Ontologies
children.blurb: Metadata and ontologies cover the structured descriptions that make research data findable, and the formal vocabularies that keep those descriptions consistent across systems.

children.name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
children.blurb: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers arrangements in which several organisations analyse a combined dataset without any one of them handing over the raw records.

children.name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
children.blurb: Institutional knowledge graphs are structured representations of an organisation's people, projects, publications, datasets, equipment and their relationships, built so that questions spanning those entities can be answered from one connected source.

children.name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
children.blurb: Long-term digital preservation covers the practices and systems that keep digital material readable and usable across decades, well past the life of the hardware and software that created it.

sections.body: Research data and repositories is the layer of artificial intelligence work that deals with the material research runs on: datasets, their descriptions, their movement between institutions, and their survival over decades. In practice, AI systems are being used to generate metadata at scale, to match schemas across disciplines, to suggest ontology terms for unlabelled fields, and to detect duplicates or inconsistencies in large collections. Machine learning also helps route access requests, classify sensitive records, and link related datasets that were catalogued under different conventions. The work is less about building clever models than about making collections findable, comparable, and usable by both people and software. It sits close to libraries, archives, and research computing groups rather than to model labs.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The principles behind FAIR data are widely accepted, and most major funders and journals now expect data to be described and deposited in some structured way. What is solved is the basic plumbing: persistent identifiers, standard citation, and common metadata vocabularies exist and are used. What is not solved is the messy middle. Ontologies still conflict across fields, automated metadata extraction is uneven in quality, and federated systems for sensitive data remain hard to run because legal and ethical review does not scale with the technology. Long-term preservation is genuinely difficult when formats, software, and institutional budgets all change. Honest limits include the fact that no automated system can decide what a dataset means to a future researcher, and that access control for sensitive data is a governance problem more than a computational one.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here form a chain from description to durability. FAIR Data sets out the principles that shape everything else, and a reader goes there first to understand what good practice means and where it is enforced. Metadata and Ontologies goes deeper into how meaning is encoded and why different communities struggle to agree, which matters when automated tools try to reconcile them. Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data addresses the hardest operational case, where data cannot simply be copied, and it is the page to read for the tension between collaboration and control. Institutional Knowledge Graphs shows how an organisation can connect its own people, projects, and outputs into something queryable, which is where AI methods contribute most visibly. Long-Term Digital Preservation closes the sequence by asking what survives, and it is the page for anyone thinking past the current grant cycle.
